Summary
Corporate resilience is a firm’s capacity to withstand and adapt to shocks while maintaining revenue, retaining capabilities, and recovering operations. The “product program” spans how large and varied a firm’s product and business portfolio is (breadth/size) and how far and in what directions that portfolio reaches (range: relatedness, technologies, geographies, and supply–customer networks). Evidence indicates that breadth and range can enhance resilience by creating redundancy, smoothing regional and sectoral shocks, and expanding access to resources and markets, but benefits diminish and risks rise when diversification exceeds managerial control or is poorly structured, yielding a non-linear, governance‑ and sector‑contingent payoff. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic dispersion can foster resilience via cash‑flow smoothing, cross‑regional supply chain continuity, and access to regional resources, but may also raise costs and invite internal disruptions</cite> <cite id="72c31408-2">Firms with high geographic dispersion showed higher total asset turnover and easier access to non‑local loans and subsidies during COVID‑19, supporting survival advantages</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Supply‑chain and customer base diversification helped Chinese manufacturers cope with and recover from COVID‑19 disruptions by reducing fragility from overreliance on few partners</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Meta‑analytic and recent empirical work shows diversification benefits increase performance and resilience up to a moderate scale, then decline with excessive, especially unrelated, diversification</cite> <cite id="72c31408-0">Concentrated supplier bases magnified pandemic‑era disruptions; diversifying suppliers across locations and capabilities improved agility and risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="b329d272-2">Horizontal diversification protected SMEs during COVID‑19 by lowering the likelihood of shutdowns, layoffs, and labor shortages relative to horizontally specialized peers</cite>.

What “size” (breadth) of the product program does
Breadth—how many products, customers, and suppliers a firm directly serves—affects resilience through redundancy and risk pooling. Multipoint exposure to multiple segments reduces the probability that a single shock wipes out revenues, and spread across multiple counterparties can stabilize cash flows and preserve operating capacity. <cite id="72c31408-3">Firms that diversified supply and customer bases recovered faster from COVID‑19 disruptions than those relying on few partners, underscoring the fragility of concentrated revenue and transaction networks</cite> <cite id="72c31408-0">Pandemic disruptions exposed the vulnerability of concentrated supplier dependency; diversifying suppliers by location and capability improved agility and adaptation</cite>. Cross‑sector evidence also links breadth to crisis survival: <cite id="b329d272-2">SMEs with higher horizontal diversification were less likely to shut down or lay off workers during COVID‑19 than horizontally specialized firms, indicating buffering against external shocks</cite>.

Limits to breadth and the risk of over‑dispersion
Diversification’s resilience payoff is not monotone. <cite id="26442d9e-1">A meta‑analysis of 263 effect sizes finds an inverted‑U: moderate diversification improves performance and adaptive capacity, while excessive diversification—especially when combined with high unrelated product diversity—undermines outcomes</cite>. Over‑dispersed portfolios strain coordination, invite agency frictions, and can create new vulnerabilities in internal supply chains. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic dispersion that fragments scale and introduces internal supply chain disruptions can heighten pandemic vulnerability, so the net resilience effect depends on managing these costs</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">SMEs with weak governance suffer diversification discounts due to agency problems and resource misallocation, eroding resilience benefits</cite>. In short, breadth helps when it is “thick” in capabilities and thin in managerial load—i.e., products that share routines, data, platforms, and governance.

What “range” (relatedness, technology scope, and geography) does
Range—how far portfolio businesses and products differ in technology and market—shapes resilience via absorptive capacity, option value, and geographic risk smoothing. Technology‑related breadth exploits economies of scope and knowledge sharing to stabilize and reconfigure offerings after shocks. <cite id="b329d272-1">Related diversification is the rule for expanding production portfolios; technologically similar products create synergies and efficiency gains, supporting faster adjustment after demand shocks</cite>. Geographic reach diversifies regional exposure and access to inputs/finances. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographically diversified portfolios smooth cash‑flow volatility from regional outbreaks, sustain operations via cross‑regional supply chains, and access cross‑regional resources, improving survival</cite> <cite id="72c31408-2">High geographic dispersion was associated with higher asset turnover and easier access to non‑local loans and subsidies in 2020, consistent with better resource mobilization during stress</cite>. Digital capabilities can amplify geographic and product reach’s resilience payoff by reducing transaction costs and enabling reconfiguration. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Digital transformation promotes corporate diversification by lowering transaction costs and financing constraints, strengthening the link between diversification breadth/relatedness and resilience</cite>.

Crisis‑era evidence: COVID‑19 and beyond
COVID‑19 sharpened trade‑offs between concentration and diversification. <cite id="72c31408-0">Automotive and other supply chains suffered when supplier concentration prevented rapid adaptation; firms with diversified supplier bases fared better</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Manufacturers with diversified supply/customer networks maintained operations and recovered faster during the pandemic, reinforcing diversification as a proactive resilience tool</cite>. International exposure also mattered for small firms. <cite id="26442d9e-3">SMEs with high international diversification had 24% higher revenue stability, 18% greater profit margin resilience, and 30% faster operational rebound post‑disruptions than domestic peers, though sectoral constraints (regulatory/cultural) limited gains for services</cite>. For SMEs and larger firms alike, horizontal diversification reduced shutdowns and labor shocks, but benefits depended on governance and financing structure. <cite id="b329d272-2">Horizontal diversification buffered against shutdowns and labor shortages in COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Moderate diversification improves outcomes; excessive, unrelated diversification weakens them</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-2">International evidence shows financially constrained SMEs diversified financing sources more than unconstrained peers in a quadratic fashion, reflecting optimal complementarity</cite>.

Mechanisms that strengthen or weaken the resilience payoff
- Resource slack and governance: <cite id="26442d9e-1">Firms with stronger governance and digital infrastructure convert diversification into resilience more effectively</cite>. Robust boards, risk functions, and long‑term orientation enable rapid reallocation across products, regions, and partners during shocks, whereas weak governance erodes benefits and invites diversification discounts. 
- Knowledge base and absorptive capacity: <cite id="b329d272-1">Technological relatedness underpins scope economies and post‑shock reconfiguration</cite>. Shared R&D, data, and manufacturing know‑how reduce adjustment costs and accelerate recovery.
- Network structure and redundancy: <cite id="72c31408-0">Diversifying suppliers across geographies and capabilities reduces single‑point failure risks</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Multiple supply and customer bases cushion disruptions and speed rebound</cite>.
- Trade‑offs: <cite id="72c31408-1">Scale economies versus internal fragility; geographic dispersion can raise coordination and internal disruption risks</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Unrelated breadth fragments capabilities and increases agency/coordination costs, undermining resilience</cite>.

Contextual moderators
Sector and shock type condition the impact of breadth and range. Technology‑intensive and manufacturing SMEs often gain more from international and supply diversification than service firms, which face regulatory and cultural frictions. <cite id="26442d9e-3">Technology‑driven and manufacturing SMEs saw larger gains from international diversification, while services faced regulatory/cultural barriers</cite>. Governance quality and digital capabilities moderate whether breadth translates into resilience. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Digital transformation strengthens diversification benefits; weak governance produces diversification penalties</cite>. Firm size matters at the margins: concentrated networks can raise efficiency and knowledge sharing in knowledge‑intensive industries, but overreliance increases systemic risk; diversified networks distribute risk and inclusivity but raise coordination and environmental footprints. <cite id="72c31408-4">Concentrated supply structures raise resource efficiency and knowledge sharing but heighten vulnerability to regional or partner shocks; diversified networks spread risk but increase coordination and carbon costs</cite>.

Putting it together: How to size and range your product program for resilience
- Calibrate breadth to capability and need. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Moderate breadth yields resilience gains; excessive, especially unrelated, breadth erodes performance</cite>. Favor depth within arenas where capabilities are strong (platforms, shared processes, data), and add new products/segments that extend rather than replace core competencies. <cite id="b329d272-1">Related diversification leverages synergies and supports rapid adjustment after shocks</cite>.
- Extend range to geographies and supply ecosystems that diversify risk without fragmenting control. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic dispersion smooths regional volatility, preserves supply relationships, and unlocks cross‑regional resources</cite> <cite id="72c31408-2">Dispersed firms accessed non‑local loans and subsidies during COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Diversified supply/customer bases supported faster recovery</cite>. Use “hub‑and‑spoke” structures with strong supplier‑onboarding, compliance, and coordination systems to mitigate internal coordination costs. <cite id="72c31408-1">Internal supply chain disruptions from dispersion can undermine resilience unless carefully managed</cite>.
- Invest in governance and digital infrastructure to monetize diversification. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Digital transformation reduces transaction costs, eases financing constraints, and strengthens diversification’s resilience payoff</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-0">Resilience‑oriented governance strengthens risk management, transparency, and long‑term strategic integration of supply‑chain dependencies</cite>.
- Monitor sectoral and shock‑era heterogeneity. <cite id="26442d9e-3">Manufacturing and tech SMEs gain more from international diversification, while services face barriers</cite>. During concentrated systemic shocks (pandemics, geopolitics), proactively diversify revenue and risk, and prepare contingency financing. <cite id="72c31408-3">Governments and firms should encourage backup suppliers/markets and provide bridge financing to support recovery</cite>.
- Guard against over‑dispersion and governance decay. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Weak governance yields diversification discounts; unrelated breadth raises agency and coordination costs</cite> <cite id="72c31408-1">Excessive dispersion can raise internal disruption risk and reduce economies of scale</cite>. Use portfolio reviews to prune low‑relatedness ventures and consolidate overlapping capabilities.

Key takeaways
- Breadth (size) helps when it builds redundancy in products, customers, and suppliers; breadth without depth can backfire under severe shocks. <cite id="72c31408-3">Diversified revenue/supply structures improved disruption coping and recovery</cite> <cite id="b329d272-2">Horizontal diversification reduced shutdowns and labor shocks</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Benefits peak at moderate breadth and decline with excessive or unrelated diversification</cite>.
- Range (relatedness and geography) amplifies resilience via knowledge sharing and regional risk smoothing, but must be balanced against coordination costs and governance quality. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic and technology range smooth volatility and preserve operations when well executed; otherwise they create new vulnerabilities</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Related diversification exploits synergies; governance and digital infrastructure are critical moderators</cite>.
- Resilience is dynamic and adaptive, not a one‑time fix; firms that combine breadth/with range with strong governance and digital capabilities recover faster and are better positioned as shocks evolve. <cite id="26442d9e-0">Resilience emerges through continuous learning, adaptation, and governance that embeds risk management and long‑term orientation</cite>.

Limitations and open questions
Evidence is strongest for geographic/supply diversification and SME‑level product breadth; fewer causal estimates quantify the failure/survival impact of portfolio size across large public firms in real time. Sectoral heterogeneity and governance/technology contingencies complicate one‑size‑fits‑all prescriptions, and internal integration costs vary by industry structure. Future work linking high‑frequency shocks to firm‑level portfolio reconfiguration and survival would sharpen guidance on optimal breadth and range under rapid change. <cite id="72c31408-1">Endogeneity and operationalization challenges persist in diversification‑resilience studies</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Measurement improvements and meta‑analytic moderation help but call for more sector‑specific causal designs</cite>.

Title: Business Resilience amid Global Crises: Between Adaptation, Innovation, and Legal Certainty
Snippet: Similarly, revenue diversification is not simply a survival strategy, but an effort to create new sources of value that remain relevant to evolving market needs (Basile, 2026). 

These findings suggest that business resilience is an evolutionary and dynamic process. Resilience does not exist as a static condition permanently attached to a particular sector or firm, but rather emerges through continuous processes of learning, adjustment, and transformation. Accordingly, business resilience is more appropriately understood as the capacity to continuously adapt in the face of uncertainty, rather than merely the ability to endure a single episode of crisis (Olubiyi, 2026). 

On the other hand, the findings of this study also carry important implications for corporate governance. Global crises have demonstrated that governance models oriented Resilience-oriented corporate governance demands the strengthening of risk management functions, transparency in decision-making processes, and the integration of long-term perspectives into corporate strategies. Boards of directors and top management are responsible not only for financial performance, but also for the organization's capacity to withstand uncertainty. In this context, strategic decision-making must take into account crisis scenarios, supply chain dependencies, and exposure to legal and reputational risks (Tariq, 2026a). 

Furthermore, sound corporate governance requires enhanced legal and regulatory literacy at the managerial level. Business resilience is determined not only by innovation and market adaptation, but also by a firm's ability to comply with and strategically utilize the legal framework. Legal compliance is not merely a normative obligation, but an integral component of risk management and stakeholder trust-building (Daodu & Bhaumik, 2024). 

Ultimately, policy implications and corporate governance converge at a critical point: the importance of synergy between the state and business actors. Sustainable business resilience can only be achieved when adaptive public policies are supported by responsive and responsible corporate governance. The state provides legal certainty and policy stability, while businesses internalize principles of prudence, transparency, and social responsibility in their operations (Lin, Xiaoyu, & Jianqiang, 2023). 

Within this framework, global crises should be understood not only as tests of economic endurance, but also as assessments of institutional quality and governance effectiveness (Holland, 2018).

Title: EVALUATING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF ENTERPRISE DIVERSIFICATION PROCESS MANAGEMENT
Snippet: In contemporary management research, diversification is increasingly interpreted not simply as expansion into new activities, but as a strategic instrument for balancing growth, risk distribution, resilience, and long-term value creation. Recent international studies demonstrate that the relationship between diversification and performance is not linear and depends on the type of diversification, firm capabilities, sectoral context, and external shocks. Choi J. et al. (2021), using machinelearning analysis of annual reports, proposed a multidimensional approach to measuring diversification and showed that diversification may be associated with higher firm value, especially when it develops within a related industry space. This study is important because it also demonstrates that inconsistent findings in earlier literature were partly caused by insufficiently precise measurement of diversification itself. 

A substantial contribution to the debate was made by Arte Larimo (2022), who conducted a meta-analysis of 263 effect sizes from 187 primary studies and found that the relationship between international diversification and firm performance follows an inverted U-shape. Their results indicate that moderate diversification may improve performance, whereas excessive diversification, particularly when combined with high or unrelated product diversity, can weaken firm outcomes. This finding is important for assessing management effectiveness because it shifts attention from the simple fact of diversification to the question of its optimal scale and structure. Research published after the COVID-19 crisis has further expanded understanding of diversification as a mechanism of resilience. Essuman et al. (2023) demonstrated that foreign diversification can strengthen firm resilience indirectly through foreign market scanning, especially in highly disruptive supply-chain environments. This research is especially relevant for the present article because it connects diversification not only with profitability, but also with adaptive capacity under crisis conditions. 

Another important direction of recent scholarship concerns the interaction between diversification and digital transformation. Wang et al. (2025) argue that digital transformation significantly promotes corporate diversification by reducing transaction costs, alleviating financing constraints, and stimulating digital innovation. Their findings suggest that diversification effectiveness increasingly depends on the quality of digital infrastructure and managerial ability to reorganise internal resources. This conclusion supports the view that diversification management in the contemporary economy should be assessed not only through financial indicators, but also through organisational and technological capabilities.
</snippet>

Title: SME Diversification and Corporate Management under China-Europe Trade Integration: A Framework for Sustainable Growth
Snippet: The relationship between diversification and SME performance has generated substantial empirical inquiry, with findings that nuance the conventional wisdom regarding diversification benefits. Existing SME studies suggest that market development and diversification strategies may improve firm performance when they are supported by adequate resources, managerial capability, and market knowledge. 

Although this evidence is drawn from the U.S. food and agriculture sector and should not be directly generalized to the China-Europe context, it provides useful comparative evidence that horizontal diversification can strengthen SME resilience under external shocks. Firms with higher levels of horizontal diversification were less likely to shut down, lay off employees, or experience labor shortages than horizontally specialized firms during the COVID-19 pandemic [10]. This finding provides compelling evidence that diversification serves as a resilience mechanism, buffering SMEs against exogenous disruptions that would otherwise threaten survival. Therefore, diversification should be understood as a potential resilience mechanism rather than a universally positive strategy. 

However, the relationship between diversification and performance is not uniformly positive. A systematic literature review on corporate governance in SMEs found a direct relationship between governance mechanisms and various aspects of SME performance, including innovation, internationalization, auditing, and risk of failure, suggesting that the performance effects of diversification are mediated by the quality of governance structures [6]. Several studies claim that firms can exploit these synergies by creating an appropriate product portfolio [2,[22][23][24][25], because product portfolios that consist of technologically similar products create efficiency gains for the firm.

Summary
Corporate resilience is a firm’s capacity to withstand and adapt to shocks while maintaining revenue, retaining capabilities, and recovering operations. The “product program” spans how large and varied a firm’s product and business portfolio is (breadth/size) and how far and in what directions that portfolio reaches (range: relatedness, technologies, geographies, and supply–customer networks). Evidence indicates that breadth and range can enhance resilience by creating redundancy, smoothing regional and sectoral shocks, and expanding access to resources and markets, but benefits diminish and risks rise when diversification exceeds managerial control or is poorly structured, yielding a non-linear, governance‑ and sector‑contingent payoff. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic dispersion can foster resilience via cash‑flow smoothing, cross‑regional supply chain continuity, and access to regional resources, but may also raise costs and invite internal disruptions</cite> <cite id="72c31408-2">Firms with high geographic dispersion showed higher total asset turnover and easier access to non‑local loans and subsidies during COVID‑19, supporting survival advantages</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Supply‑chain and customer base diversification helped Chinese manufacturers cope with and recover from COVID‑19 disruptions by reducing fragility from overreliance on few partners</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Meta‑analytic and recent empirical work shows diversification benefits increase performance and resilience up to a moderate scale, then decline with excessive, especially unrelated, diversification</cite> <cite id="72c31408-0">Concentrated supplier bases magnified pandemic‑era disruptions; diversifying suppliers across locations and capabilities improved agility and risk mitigation</cite> <cite id="b329d272-2">Horizontal diversification protected SMEs during COVID‑19 by lowering the likelihood of shutdowns, layoffs, and labor shortages relative to horizontally specialized peers</cite>.

What “size” (breadth) of the product program does
Breadth—how many products, customers, and suppliers a firm directly serves—affects resilience through redundancy and risk pooling. Multipoint exposure to multiple segments reduces the probability that a single shock wipes out revenues, and spread across multiple counterparties can stabilize cash flows and preserve operating capacity. <cite id="72c31408-3">Firms that diversified supply and customer bases recovered faster from COVID‑19 disruptions than those relying on few partners, underscoring the fragility of concentrated revenue and transaction networks</cite> <cite id="72c31408-0">Pandemic disruptions exposed the vulnerability of concentrated supplier dependency; diversifying suppliers by location and capability improved agility and adaptation</cite>. Cross‑sector evidence also links breadth to crisis survival: <cite id="b329d272-2">SMEs with higher horizontal diversification were less likely to shut down or lay off workers during COVID‑19 than horizontally specialized firms, indicating buffering against external shocks</cite>.

Limits to breadth and the risk of over‑dispersion
Diversification’s resilience payoff is not monotone. <cite id="26442d9e-1">A meta‑analysis of 263 effect sizes finds an inverted‑U: moderate diversification improves performance and adaptive capacity, while excessive diversification—especially when combined with high unrelated product diversity—undermines outcomes</cite>. Over‑dispersed portfolios strain coordination, invite agency frictions, and can create new vulnerabilities in internal supply chains. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic dispersion that fragments scale and introduces internal supply chain disruptions can heighten pandemic vulnerability, so the net resilience effect depends on managing these costs</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">SMEs with weak governance suffer diversification discounts due to agency problems and resource misallocation, eroding resilience benefits</cite>. In short, breadth helps when it is “thick” in capabilities and thin in managerial load—i.e., products that share routines, data, platforms, and governance.

What “range” (relatedness, technology scope, and geography) does
Range—how far portfolio businesses and products differ in technology and market—shapes resilience via absorptive capacity, option value, and geographic risk smoothing. Technology‑related breadth exploits economies of scope and knowledge sharing to stabilize and reconfigure offerings after shocks. <cite id="b329d272-1">Related diversification is the rule for expanding production portfolios; technologically similar products create synergies and efficiency gains, supporting faster adjustment after demand shocks</cite>. Geographic reach diversifies regional exposure and access to inputs/finances. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographically diversified portfolios smooth cash‑flow volatility from regional outbreaks, sustain operations via cross‑regional supply chains, and access cross‑regional resources, improving survival</cite> <cite id="72c31408-2">High geographic dispersion was associated with higher asset turnover and easier access to non‑local loans and subsidies in 2020, consistent with better resource mobilization during stress</cite>. Crisis‑era evidence: COVID‑19 and beyond

For SMEs and larger firms alike, horizontal diversification reduced shutdowns and labor shocks, but benefits depended on governance and financing structure. <cite id="b329d272-2">Horizontal diversification buffered against shutdowns and labor shortages in COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Moderate diversification improves outcomes; excessive, unrelated diversification weakens them</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-2">International evidence shows financially constrained SMEs diversified financing sources more than unconstrained peers in a quadratic fashion, reflecting optimal complementarity</cite>.

Mechanisms that strengthen or weaken the resilience payoff

- Network structure and redundancy: <cite id="72c31408-0">Diversifying suppliers across geographies and capabilities reduces single‑point failure risks</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Multiple supply and customer bases cushion disruptions and speed rebound</cite>.
- Trade‑offs: <cite id="72c31408-1">Scale economies versus internal fragility; geographic dispersion can raise coordination and internal disruption risks</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Unrelated breadth fragments capabilities and increases agency/coordination costs, undermining resilience</cite>.

Technology‑intensive and manufacturing SMEs often gain more from international and supply diversification than service firms, which face regulatory and cultural frictions. <cite id="26442d9e-3">Technology‑driven and manufacturing SMEs saw larger gains from international diversification, while services faced regulatory/cultural barriers</cite>. Governance quality and digital capabilities moderate whether breadth translates into resilience. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Digital transformation strengthens diversification benefits; weak governance produces diversification penalties</cite>. Firm size matters at the margins: concentrated networks can raise efficiency and knowledge sharing in knowledge‑intensive industries, but overreliance increases systemic risk; diversified networks distribute risk and inclusivity but raise coordination and environmental footprints. <cite id="72c31408-4">Concentrated supply structures raise resource efficiency and knowledge sharing but heighten vulnerability to regional or partner shocks; diversified networks spread risk but increase coordination and carbon costs</cite>.

- Extend range to geographies and supply ecosystems that diversify risk without fragmenting control. <cite id="72c31408-1">Geographic dispersion smooths regional volatility, preserves supply relationships, and unlocks cross‑regional resources</cite> <cite id="72c31408-2">Dispersed firms accessed non‑local loans and subsidies during COVID‑19</cite> <cite id="72c31408-3">Diversified supply/customer bases supported faster recovery</cite>. Use “hub‑and‑spoke” structures with strong supplier‑onboarding, compliance, and coordination systems to mitigate internal coordination costs. <cite id="72c31408-1">Internal supply chain disruptions from dispersion can undermine resilience unless carefully managed</cite>.

- Monitor sectoral and shock‑era heterogeneity. <cite id="26442d9e-3">Manufacturing and tech SMEs gain more from international diversification, while services face barriers</cite>. During concentrated systemic shocks (pandemics, geopolitics), proactively diversify revenue and risk, and prepare contingency financing. <cite id="72c31408-3">Governments and firms should encourage backup suppliers/markets and provide bridge financing to support recovery</cite>.
- Guard against over‑dispersion and governance decay. <cite id="26442d9e-1">Weak governance yields diversification discounts; unrelated breadth raises agency and coordination costs</cite> <cite id="72c31408-1">Excessive dispersion can raise internal disruption risk and reduce economies of scale</cite>. Use portfolio reviews to prune low‑relatedness ventures and consolidate overlapping capabilities.

Key takeaways
- Breadth (size) helps when it builds redundancy in products, customers, and suppliers; breadth without depth can backfire under severe shocks. <cite id="72c31408-3">Diversified revenue/supply structures improved disruption coping and recovery</cite> <cite id="b329d272-2">Horizontal diversification reduced shutdowns and labor shocks</cite> <cite id="26442d9e-1">Benefits peak at moderate breadth and decline with excessive or unrelated diversification</cite>.

Sectoral heterogeneity and governance/technology contingencies complicate one‑size‑fits‑all prescriptions, and internal integration costs vary by industry structure. Title: Risk Management in Supply Chains: Strategies to Minimize Disruption
Snippet: A multi-faceted approach to supply chain management necessitates the diversification of suppliers to mitigate risks associated with disruptions. By distributing procurement across various suppliers, companies can reduce dependency on single sources that may be vulnerable to geopolitical issues, natural disasters, or pandemics. During the COVID-19 pandemic, for instance, many organizations faced significant interruptions due to their concentrated supplier bases, exposing weaknesses in their operational strategies. In the automotive industry, the strained supply chains highlighted the need for agile supplier networks capable of quickly adapting to rapid shifts in demand and environmental conditions. As assessed in recent research, barriers to effective disruption mitigation often stem from cultural factors and national differences, emphasizing the importance of developing a broad and adaptable supplier base to enhance resilience against future upheavals (Kumar et al., 2016). Implementing a diversification strategy requires careful consideration of a suppliers' geographical location and operational capabilities. Firms should evaluate not only the financial stability and production capacity of their suppliers but also their ability to respond to unforeseen disruptions. For instance, Hofstede's national cultural dimensions suggest that companies operating in cultures characterized by lower uncertainty avoidance may be more adept at navigating supply chain crises, as their operational frameworks are naturally more flexible. Consequently, diversifying suppliers across various countries can enhance a firm's agility and foster smoother adaptation during times of crisis. Such a strategy not only strengthens the supply chains resilience but also expands a company's access to diverse markets and innovations, which can prove beneficial for long-term sustainability and competitiveness (Kumar et al., 2016) Moreover, the consequences of insufficient supplier diversification extend beyond immediate disruptions and can influence long-term strategic positioning. Organizations committed to fostering diversified supply chains are better equipped to manage risk and leverage opportunities arising from unexpected trends in the market. As evidenced by the challenges encountered in the automotive sector during the pandemic, companies that had not diversified their sources faced detrimental impacts on their viability and market share. Learning from these experiences can help managers appreciate the significance of diversification as a proactive strategy rather than a reactive one.

Title: Geographic dispersion and corporate resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic
Snippet: These heterogeneous results can be attributed to the challenges of controlling for the potential endogeneity of corporate diversification (Campa & Kedia, 2002). A recent strand of the literature on corporate diversification has alleviated the endogeneity problems by investigating the performance of conglomerate firms around times of financial crisis (Almeida, Kim, & Kim, 2015;Kuppuswamy & Villalonga, 2016;Matvos & Seru, 2014;Matvos, Seru, & Silva, 2018). But they mainly focus on business diversification, and even the setting financial crisis can not provide evidence for the exclusive role of geographic dispersion. Enlighted by the previous literature, we noticed that the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic is a good setting to test the advantages of geographic dispersion which may be overlooked in usual. 

Geographic dispersion plays a positive role in fostering corporate resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic via three possible channels: 

(1) geographically diversified portfolios may smoothen the cash flow volatility caused by regional COVID-19 outbreaks; (2) geographically dispersed subsidiaries can simplify the maintenance of cross-regional supply chain relationships by firms, resulting in lower losses in firms' production and operations during the pandemic; and (3) geographic dispersion can help firms overcome the barriers of market fragmentation and obtain cross-regional market resources to better survive the pandemic. However, geographic dispersion may also result in higher costs by reducing economies of scale and increasing the possibility of internal supply chain disruptions, thereby making firms vulnerable to the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, whether geographic dispersion can make firms resilient during the COVID-19 pandemic remains an empirical question. 

We believe that China is an ideal setting in which to conduct our study for the following reasons. First, China is the largest emerging economy in the world and has a vast domestic market that provides sufficient space for firms' geographically diversified development (Ma, Tong, & Fitza, 2013). At the same time, both the unified national system and sufficient fragmentation exist among China's regional markets, creating favorable conditions for researchers to identify the role of firms' geographical dispersion.

Title: Geographic dispersion and corporate resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic
Snippet: We also find a positive association between geographic dispersion and total asset turnover, which supports our argument that geographic dispersion helps firms maintain crossregional supply chain relationships and thus leads to lower revenue losses. Moreover, we find that firms with high geographic dispersion obtained more non-local loans and government subsidies in 2020, which supports the claim that geographic dispersion has helped firms better access the resources that are crucial for survival after the pandemic. 

Our findings significantly contribute to the literature. First, our results complement the findings of relevant literature on how certain internal characteristics have helped firms develop resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic. A growing pool of evidence explores many firm characteristics that may be associated with corporate resilience during the COVID-19 pandemic, including sufficient financing (Ding et al., 2021;Fahlenbrach et al., 2021;Ramelli & Wagner, 2020), low risk exposure through the global supply chain (Ding et al., 2021), more corporate social responsibility activities (Albuquerque et al., 2020;Ding et al., 2021), a strong corporate culture (Li et al., 2021), greater employee satisfaction (Shan & Tang, 2020), better corporate governance (Amore et al., 2022;Ding et al., 2021) and more investments in intangible assets (Demers et al., 2021). We complement the findings of these studies by highlighting the positive roles of geographic dispersion in building corporate resilience and by revealing the underlying channels. 

Second, our findings contribute to the existing literature on the consequences of diversification. Whether firms should diversify is a classic issue in economics and management (Ansoff, 1957;Marshall, 1890;Smith, 1776), while most of the existing literature only focuses on the consequences of business diversification (to name but a few, Denis, Denis, & Sarin, 1997;Campa & Kedia, 2002). The increasing popularity of foreign direct investment had lifted many researchers' spirits to investigate the international diversification of multinational enterprises and its association with firm performance (Capar & Kotabe, 2003;Hitt et al., 1997) and firm risk (Olibe et al., 2008;Rugman, 1976).

Title: The effects of supply chain diversification during the COVID-19 crisis: Evidence from Chinese manufacturers
Snippet: This research used the COVID-19 context and offered operational managers implications to build resilience. Scholars (e.g., Sharma et al. 2020) and consultants (e.g., Deloitte, 2020) have suggested that firms diversify the supply chain to mitigate supply chain risk and disruption. This research provided evidence and showed that firms with a diversified supply chain have an advantage in coping with Y. Lin et al. and recovering from disruption. With the prospect of dynamism in the future business environment, managers should revisit their supply and revenue structure. Although transacting with few suppliers and customers can save firms very substantial coordination costs, these firms can be fragile when any failures happen to their supply chain partners. Despite the suggestion to diversify supply and customer bases geographically, we recommend that operational managers consider diversifying in terms of dependence on supply chain partners, avoiding overreliance on few suppliers or customers. 

The resilience of manufacturing sectors has become a vital aspect of competitiveness. Our results suggest that governments should encourage firms to have backup suppliers and markets. For example, the government can build platforms for firms to search for suitable suppliers and customers, which facilitates supply-demand matches in periods of disruption. In addition, bridge loans are essential for firms that suffered serious disruptions during COVID-19. Organizations committed to fostering diversified supply chains are better equipped to manage risk and leverage opportunities arising from unexpected trends in the market. As evidenced by the challenges encountered in the automotive sector during the pandemic, companies that had not diversified their sources faced detrimental impacts on their viability and market share. Title: Business Resilience amid Global Crises: Between Adaptation, Innovation, and Legal Certainty
Snippet: Similarly, revenue diversification is not simply a survival strategy, but an effort to create new sources of value that remain relevant to evolving market needs (Basile, 2026). 

These findings suggest that business resilience is an evolutionary and dynamic process. Resilience does not exist as a static condition permanently attached to a particular sector or firm, but rather emerges through continuous processes of learning, adjustment, and transformation. Accordingly, business resilience is more appropriately understood as the capacity to continuously adapt in the face of uncertainty, rather than merely the ability to endure a single episode of crisis (Olubiyi, 2026). 

On the other hand, the findings of this study also carry important implications for corporate governance. Global crises have demonstrated that governance models oriented Resilience-oriented corporate governance demands the strengthening of risk management functions, transparency in decision-making processes, and the integration of long-term perspectives into corporate strategies. Boards of directors and top management are responsible not only for financial performance, but also for the organization's capacity to withstand uncertainty. In this context, strategic decision-making must take into account crisis scenarios, supply chain dependencies, and exposure to legal and reputational risks (Tariq, 2026a). 

Furthermore, sound corporate governance requires enhanced legal and regulatory literacy at the managerial level. Business resilience is determined not only by innovation and market adaptation, but also by a firm's ability to comply with and strategically utilize the legal framework. Legal compliance is not merely a normative obligation, but an integral component of risk management and stakeholder trust-building (Daodu & Bhaumik, 2024). 

Ultimately, policy implications and corporate governance converge at a critical point: the importance of synergy between the state and business actors. Sustainable business resilience can only be achieved when adaptive public policies are supported by responsive and responsible corporate governance. The state provides legal certainty and policy stability, while businesses internalize principles of prudence, transparency, and social responsibility in their operations (Lin, Xiaoyu, & Jianqiang, 2023). 

Within this framework, global crises should be understood not only as tests of economic endurance, but also as assessments of institutional quality and governance effectiveness (Holland, 2018).

Title: EVALUATING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF ENTERPRISE DIVERSIFICATION PROCESS MANAGEMENT
Snippet: In contemporary management research, diversification is increasingly interpreted not simply as expansion into new activities, but as a strategic instrument for balancing growth, risk distribution, resilience, and long-term value creation. Recent international studies demonstrate that the relationship between diversification and performance is not linear and depends on the type of diversification, firm capabilities, sectoral context, and external shocks. Choi J. et al. (2021), using machinelearning analysis of annual reports, proposed a multidimensional approach to measuring diversification and showed that diversification may be associated with higher firm value, especially when it develops within a related industry space. This study is important because it also demonstrates that inconsistent findings in earlier literature were partly caused by insufficiently precise measurement of diversification itself. 

A substantial contribution to the debate was made by Arte Larimo (2022), who conducted a meta-analysis of 263 effect sizes from 187 primary studies and found that the relationship between international diversification and firm performance follows an inverted U-shape. Their results indicate that moderate diversification may improve performance, whereas excessive diversification, particularly when combined with high or unrelated product diversity, can weaken firm outcomes. This finding is important for assessing management effectiveness because it shifts attention from the simple fact of diversification to the question of its optimal scale and structure. Research published after the COVID-19 crisis has further expanded understanding of diversification as a mechanism of resilience. Essuman et al. (2023) demonstrated that foreign diversification can strengthen firm resilience indirectly through foreign market scanning, especially in highly disruptive supply-chain environments. This research is especially relevant for the present article because it connects diversification not only with profitability, but also with adaptive capacity under crisis conditions. 

Another important direction of recent scholarship concerns the interaction between diversification and digital transformation. Wang et al. (2025) argue that digital transformation significantly promotes corporate diversification by reducing transaction costs, alleviating financing constraints, and stimulating digital innovation. Their findings suggest that diversification effectiveness increasingly depends on the quality of digital infrastructure and managerial ability to reorganise internal resources. This conclusion supports the view that diversification management in the contemporary economy should be assessed not only through financial indicators, but also through organisational and technological capabilities.

Title: SME Diversification and Corporate Management under China-Europe Trade Integration: A Framework for Sustainable Growth
Snippet: The relationship between diversification and SME performance has generated substantial empirical inquiry, with findings that nuance the conventional wisdom regarding diversification benefits. Existing SME studies suggest that market development and diversification strategies may improve firm performance when they are supported by adequate resources, managerial capability, and market knowledge. 

Although this evidence is drawn from the U.S. food and agriculture sector and should not be directly generalized to the China-Europe context, it provides useful comparative evidence that horizontal diversification can strengthen SME resilience under external shocks. Firms with higher levels of horizontal diversification were less likely to shut down, lay off employees, or experience labor shortages than horizontally specialized firms during the COVID-19 pandemic [10]. This finding provides compelling evidence that diversification serves as a resilience mechanism, buffering SMEs against exogenous disruptions that would otherwise threaten survival. Therefore, diversification should be understood as a potential resilience mechanism rather than a universally positive strategy. 

However, the relationship between diversification and performance is not uniformly positive. A systematic literature review on corporate governance in SMEs found a direct relationship between governance mechanisms and various aspects of SME performance, including innovation, internationalization, auditing, and risk of failure, suggesting that the performance effects of diversification are mediated by the quality of governance structures [6]. SMEs with weak governance may experience diversification discount __ the phenomenon where diversified firms trade at lower valuation multiples than focused firms __ due to agency problems, coordination costs, and resource misallocation. 

International evidence from cross-country SME samples indicates that SMEs experiencing a moderate degree of financial constraints use the most diversified sources of financing, while financially unconstrained SMEs use fewer financing sources [11]. This quadratic relationship suggests that diversification of financing sources by SMEs is a strategic choice based on optimal complementarity achieved through credit multiplier channels, rather than a desperate response to financial distress.

Title: Assessing the Role of International Diversification in Enhancing SME Resilience: A Comparative Analysis
Snippet: Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) face increasing financial risks and market volatility, making resilience a
critical factor for their long-term survival and growth. International diversification has been proposed as a strategic tool to
enhance SME resilience by reducing dependency on domestic markets, spreading risks, and accessing new growth opportunities.
This study conducts a comparative analysis of SMEs with varying degrees of international exposure to assess the effectiveness of
diversification in mitigating financial and operational risks. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study examines financial
performance metrics, market adaptability, and risk management strategies of 200 SMEs across multiple industries. Quantitative
data, sourced from financial reports and trade records, were analysed alongside qualitative insights from SME managers
through structured interviews. Results indicate that SMEs with a high level of international diversification exhibit 24% higher
revenue stability and 18% greater profit margin resilience during economic downturns compared to their domestically focused
counterparts. Additionally, these firms demonstrate superior crisis recovery capabilities, with 30% faster operational rebound
post-disruptions. Sectoral differences were observed, with technology-driven and manufacturing SMEs benefiting more
significantly from international expansion, while service-oriented firms faced greater challenges due to regulatory and cultural
barriers. Key challenges identified include resource constraints, trade policy complexities, and market entry barriers, which limit
the effectiveness of diversification for smaller firms. This study provides empirical evidence on the strategic benefits of
international diversification for SMEs, offering practical recommendations for policymakers and business leaders to optimize
international expansion and enhance firm resilience in uncertain economic environments.

Title: Defining the Determinants of Corporate Financial Performance: A Machine Learning Approach
Snippet: Frequently traditional frameworks inadequately model how internal factors (e.g., liquidity) and external shocks (e.g., sanctions) interactively amplify or mitigate risks. For instance, corporate social responsibility's (CSR) role may shift from profit-enhancing to survival-critical under sanctions [22,23], a transition stakeholder theory attributes to shifting salience among competing claims [14] as firms prioritize short-term legitimacy over long-term ethics [24] -a dynamic linear models fail to disentangle. Aksoy and Yilmaz (2024) [23] further emphasize the moderating role of sustainability performance in crisis resilience, revealing that firms with robust ESG practices mitigated pandemic-induced financial losses more effectively. 

While sector-specific vulnerabilities are acknowledged [25], predictive analytics under systemic shocks are rare. Institutional theory [6,26] suggests firms in crisis adopt isomorphic survival strategies during institutional transitions, yet such adaptations remain poorly quantified. Russia's post-2022 environment, marked by abrupt supply chain disruptions and ownership restructuring [27,28], demands tools that handle high-dimensional, noisy data [29]. Despite ML's rise in finance, few studies employ ensemble techniques to improve robustness in CFP prediction, particularly in sanction-affected contexts where evolutionary adaptations occur. Hsu et al. (2025) [21] advance this discourse by integrating ESG metrics into deep learning frameworks, demonstrating enhanced predictive accuracy for firms operating in regulated industries. Stewardship theory [30] posits that managerial autonomy enhances resilience, but existing models lack the granularity to test this in high-stakes environments. Ensemble models, which aggregate multiple algorithms (e.g., Random Forests, Gradient Boosting), remain untapped for isolating key drivers of financial resilience. 

The aim of this paper is twofold: First, to empirically identify the non-linear, crisis-driven interactions between CFP determinants -including R&D, CSR, leverage, and industry dynamics -in Russia's post-2022 sanction context, using ensemble ML to overcome limitations of traditional econometrics.

The relationship between diversification and SME performance has generated substantial empirical inquiry, with findings that nuance the conventional wisdom regarding diversification benefits. Existing SME studies suggest that market development and diversification strategies may improve firm performance when they are supported by adequate resources, managerial capability, and market knowledge.

Firms with higher levels of horizontal diversification were less likely to shut down, lay off employees, or experience labor shortages than horizontally specialized firms during the COVID-19 pandemic [10]. This finding provides compelling evidence that diversification serves as a resilience mechanism, buffering SMEs against exogenous disruptions that would otherwise threaten survival. Therefore, diversification should be understood as a potential resilience mechanism rather than a universally positive strategy. 

However, the relationship between diversification and performance is not uniformly positive. A systematic literature review on corporate governance in SMEs found a direct relationship between governance mechanisms and various aspects of SME performance, including innovation, internationalization, auditing, and risk of failure, suggesting that the performance effects of diversification are mediated by the quality of governance structures [6]. SMEs with weak governance may experience diversification discount __ the phenomenon where diversified firms trade at lower valuation multiples than focused firms __ due to agency problems, coordination costs, and resource misallocation. 

International evidence from cross-country SME samples indicates that SMEs experiencing a moderate degree of financial constraints use the most diversified sources of financing, while financially unconstrained SMEs use fewer financing sources [11]. This quadratic relationship suggests that diversification of financing sources by SMEs is a strategic choice based on optimal complementarity achieved through credit multiplier channels, rather than a desperate response to financial distress.

Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) face increasing financial risks and market volatility, making resilience a
critical factor for their long-term survival and growth. International diversification has been proposed as a strategic tool to
enhance SME resilience by reducing dependency on domestic markets, spreading risks, and accessing new growth opportunities.
This study conducts a comparative analysis of SMEs with varying degrees of international exposure to assess the effectiveness of
diversification in mitigating financial and operational risks. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study examines financial
performance metrics, market adaptability, and risk management strategies of 200 SMEs across multiple industries. Quantitative
data, sourced from financial reports and trade records, were analysed alongside qualitative insights from SME managers
through structured interviews. Results indicate that SMEs with a high level of international diversification exhibit 24% higher
revenue stability and 18% greater profit margin resilience during economic downturns compared to their domestically focused
counterparts. Additionally, these firms demonstrate superior crisis recovery capabilities, with 30% faster operational rebound
post-disruptions. Sectoral differences were observed, with technology-driven and manufacturing SMEs benefiting more
significantly from international expansion, while service-oriented firms faced greater challenges due to regulatory and cultural
barriers. Key challenges identified include resource constraints, trade policy complexities, and market entry barriers, which limit
the effectiveness of diversification for smaller firms. This study provides empirical evidence on the strategic benefits of
international diversification for SMEs, offering practical recommendations for policymakers and business leaders to optimize
international expansion and enhance firm resilience in uncertain economic environments.

Snippet: The purpose of this study is to look into the relationship between Pakistani firms' performance and product diversity. The basic reason for this study is that diversification of related and unrelated products inside the portfolio of a business of operations allow the organization to perform better. Both primary and secondary data was collected. A census 75 manufacturing firms was taken. Secondary data was acquired from these firms' annual reports during a two-year period. Questionnaires from 303 departmental managers were submitted. Stata was used to provide descriptive summaries and do regression analysis on the data. According to this study, there is a significant relationship between product diversification and firm performance. Both related and unrelated product diversification strategies can be useful in enhancing a company's success. While unrelated diversification can create new revenue streams and lessen the likelihood of market consolidation, related diversification can benefit from the resources already available.

Title: Related adjustment of firm production after demand shocks
Snippet: Multiproduct firms are thought to exploit economies of scope by diversifying into technologically similar activities because they are motivated to introduce new products that require relatively few extra investments [1][2][3]. Technological similarities, also termed technological relatedness [4], are therefore of central concern in strategic decision of firms and in a wide variety of distinct economics literature including firm expansion, international development, and regional diversification [1,[5][6][7][8]. A growing body of empirical evidence suggests that related diversification of firms is the rule of expanding production portfolio [4,[7][8][9][10][11][12][13]. Further, the same logic has been applied to explain the development of industries [14][15][16], countries [17,18] and regions [19,20] by claiming that these units diversify easier to technologically related activities than to unrelated ones (for a recent review see [21]). 

The synergies and complementarities across production classified in different industries is the major underlying argument behind the principle of relatedness. Several studies claim that firms can exploit these synergies by creating an appropriate product portfolio [2,[22][23][24][25], because product portfolios that consist of technologically similar products create efficiency gains for the firm. 

Nevertheless, there are also many multi-product firms that produce technologically nonsimilar products. Nathanson and Cassano [26], for example, have found nearly the same number of firms with related and unrelated product portfolios. A key motivation for such portfolio may be that unrelated diversification is associated with resilience against industry-specific shocks both for firms [27] and for regions [28]. 

Our aim in this paper is to better understand the dynamics of related and unrelated diversification of firms. The question is, under what conditions do firms diversify into related activities and increase the coherence of their product portfolio, and when do they diversify into unrelated products? Although the question about the dynamics of diversification was raised long ago [29], we have few systematic empirical evidence on the factors that facilitate related versus unrelated diversification of firms' production.

documents.title: Firm Performance Outcomes of Product Diversification Strategies in Pakistan
documents.snippet: The purpose of this study is to look into the relationship between Pakistani firms' performance and product diversity. The basic reason for this study is that diversification of related and unrelated products inside the portfolio of a business of operations allow the organization to perform better. Both primary and secondary data was collected. A census 75 manufacturing firms was taken. Secondary data was acquired from these firms' annual reports during a two-year period. Questionnaires from 303 departmental managers were submitted. Stata was used to provide descriptive summaries and do regression analysis on the data. According to this study, there is a significant relationship between product diversification and firm performance. Both related and unrelated product diversification strategies can be useful in enhancing a company's success. While unrelated diversification can create new revenue streams and lessen the likelihood of market consolidation, related diversification can benefit from the resources already available.

documents.snippet:
Multiproduct firms are thought to exploit economies of scope by diversifying into technologically similar activities because they are motivated to introduce new products that require relatively few extra investments [1][2][3]. Technological similarities, also termed technological relatedness [4], are therefore of central concern in strategic decision of firms and in a wide variety of distinct economics literature including firm expansion, international development, and regional diversification [1,[5][6][7][8]. A growing body of empirical evidence suggests that related diversification of firms is the rule of expanding production portfolio [4,[7][8][9][10][11][12][13]. Further, the same logic has been applied to explain the development of industries [14][15][16], countries [17,18] and regions [19,20] by claiming that these units diversify easier to technologically related activities than to unrelated ones (for a recent review see [21]). 

The synergies and complementarities across production classified in different industries is the major underlying argument behind the principle of relatedness. Several studies claim that firms can exploit these synergies by creating an appropriate product portfolio [2,[22][23][24][25], because product portfolios that consist of technologically similar products create efficiency gains for the firm. 

Nevertheless, there are also many multi-product firms that produce technologically nonsimilar products. Nathanson and Cassano [26], for example, have found nearly the same number of firms with related and unrelated product portfolios. A key motivation for such portfolio may be that unrelated diversification is associated with resilience against industry-specific shocks both for firms [27] and for regions [28]. 

Our aim in this paper is to better understand the dynamics of related and unrelated diversification of firms. The question is, under what conditions do firms diversify into related activities and increase the coherence of their product portfolio, and when do they diversify into unrelated products? Although the question about the dynamics of diversification was raised long ago [29], we have few systematic empirical evidence on the factors that facilitate related versus unrelated diversification of firms' production.

Summary answer
- Breadth (range) and scale (size) of product programs shape resilience through risk-spreading, option value, resource reallocation, and dependency reduction, but effects are often non‑linear and contingent on relatedness, modularity, and governance. <cite id="02f4d533-0">Diversification reduces concentration in products/markets, supports reallocation, and creates option value that helps firms pivot during shocks</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-3">Diversified product portfolios reduce dependency on specific inputs and buyers, improving continuity during disruptions</cite>. <cite id="02f4d533-1,ff1f28e6-0">Empirical studies frequently find an inverse U‑shaped relation: moderate breadth yields the highest resilience, with both too little and too much breadth penalizing performance</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-2">Quadratic effects of portfolio breadth on firm survival are robust, with mid-sized breadth outperforming small and large breadth</cite>. <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">Related diversification leverages coherent capabilities and can raise resilience; unrelated breadth without fit risks inefficiency</cite>. 
- Comparability across studies is limited by differing definitions (breadth vs. variety vs. SKU counts vs. coherence), metrics (survival, recovery, profitability, innovation outcomes), time windows (pandemic vs. longer panels), and contexts (industry concentration, GVC position), but cross‑literature patterns cohere: moderate breadth plus aligned capabilities and modularity tends to improve resilience; extreme breadth or misaligned breadth undermines it. <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Diversification effectiveness depends on matching form of diversification, resource capacity, sectoral environment, and managerial timeliness</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-1">Inverse U‑shaped effects and R&D interactions vary by ownership and environmental stress</cite>.

1. Concepts: product‑program size and range
- Product‑program “size” can refer to the number of products, concurrent SKUs, or the scale of the firm’s product base and R&D effort across platforms; “range” refers to breadth/diversification—variety across product categories, customer segments, geographies, or technology domains—and coherence/relatedness among offerings. <cite id="02f4d533-0">Diversification spreads risk across product lines, customer segments, and markets, reducing localized demand shocks</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-1">Coherent diversification emphasizes relatedness and network structure across products and countries</cite>. 
- In operations and supply chains, “range” also appears as product assortment breadth and supplier base breadth; “size” as SKU count, facility specialization, or order quantity scale. <cite id="06149198-3">Beauty and personal care retailers mitigated pandemic disruptions by focusing on multiple brands, bulk ordering, and stronger supplier cooperation</cite> <cite id="06149198-2">Simulation evidence for online grocery shows backup suppliers and capacity increases restored performance under disruptions</cite>.

2. Breadth (range) and resilience: mechanisms and quantitative evidence
- Mechanisms: risk pooling, flexibility, and dependency reduction. <cite id="02f4d533-0">Diversified firms can shift resources from contracting to expanding activities, maintaining utilization and employment during shocks, and gain option value to scale quickly into promising segments</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-3">Within global value chains, product diversification reduces dependence on single buyers or inputs, stabilizing production and margins</cite>. 
- Cross‑sector and cross‑country evidence. <cite id="02f4d533-0">Comparative evidence from U.S. food/agriculture during COVID shows diversified firms were less likely to shut down, lay off workers, or face labor shortages than horizontally specialized peers</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-0">Enterprises selling domestically and internationally achieved higher sales growth in downturns than single‑market firms, especially in concentrated industries</cite>. 
- Non‑linear (inverted‑U) patterns and dynamic stress tests. <cite id="02f4d533-1">In Chinese high‑tech listed firms under U.S. sanctions, product diversification exhibits an inverse U‑shaped relationship with resilience; R&D increases have diminishing returns and amplify the inverted‑U effect, with stronger impacts for non‑state‑owned firms</cite>. <cite id="02f4d533-2">In resource‑constrained renewable natural resource industries, survival time increases with moderate portfolio breadth and declines at very high breadth, with a robust quadratic fit and higher explained variance</cite>. <cite id="ff1f28e6-4">Patent portfolio diversity also shows inverted‑U links to profitability at the industry level</cite>. 
- Related vs. unrelated breadth and capability alignment. <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">Firms with high technology intensity benefit from higher patent diversity; low‑tech firms may be better off specializing</cite>. <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Related diversification cases (Apple, Amazon, Tesla, Salomon) produced broader ecosystems, diversified revenues, stronger positions, and greater strategic resilience, but effects weaken when scope/complexity exceed managerial capacity</cite>. 
- Supply chain breadth under disruptions. <cite id="06149198-3">Beauty and personal care retailers improved resilience by broadening brand sources, bulk purchasing, and credit/cash terms and maintaining intensive supplier interaction</cite> <cite id="06149198-2">Backup suppliers and capacity upgrades restored profits and reduced lead time in simulations</cite> <cite id="06149198-1">Shorter, multi‑source local supply chains showed greater resilience than long, specialized chains in rural Australia during COVID‑related shocks</cite> <cite id="06149198-4">Beef sector disruptions highlighted fragility of specialized, inflexible supply chains and suggested resilience levers like multi‑purpose facilities, labor/management changes, and inventory redesign</cite>. 
- Product development capability as a resilience amplifier. <cite id="02f4d533-4">Resilient SMEs in clusters heavily used product development to pivot (70% of resilient firms vs. 35% of non‑resilient), leveraging core competencies to shift lines into hygiene/medical fabrics, maintaining or increasing turnover</cite>.

3. Size (scale) of product programs and R&D intensity
- Scale interacts with breadth: modest scale supports flexibility; excessive scale can create inflexibility or sunk costs. <cite id="02f4d533-1">R&D investment improves resilience with diminishing returns and interacts multiplicatively with the inverse‑U breadth effect, amplifying penalties outside an optimal “double threshold” range</cite>. <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">Patent diversity exhibits inverted‑U effects on innovation and profitability, implying that too much or too little variety is suboptimal</cite>. 
- Portfolio composition matters. <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Effectiveness hinges on matching diversification form (related vs. unrelated) to resources, environment, and managerial capacity; otherwise, breadth can add costs without resilience gains</cite>. 
- Scale in operations: SKU and facility breadth versus specialization. <cite id="06149198-1">Large chains gained preferential disaster‑response access, but specialization and long chains increased vulnerability; diversifying suppliers/shortening chains improved resilience</cite> <cite id="06149198-2">Increasing centralized fulfillment center capacity and adopting priority slots mitigated disruption costs in simulations</cite>. 
- Strategic amplifiers. <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">Technology leaders strategically allocating R&D and building patent roadmaps outperformed rivals by balancing variety and coherence</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-1">Under sanctions, R&D buffering enhanced resilience but with diminishing returns, and complemented optimal breadth</cite>.

4. Supply chain and operations perspective: SKU/assortment and dependency breadth
- Assortment breadth can hedge against category‑specific shocks but raises coordination and inventory costs. <cite id="06149198-3">Pandemic‑era strategies in beauty/personal care emphasized multi‑brand breadth and cooperation to maintain supply and meet fluctuating demand</cite>. <cite id="06149198-2">Rationing slots and bulk ordering softened demand/lead‑time impacts; backup suppliers restored baseline profits</cite>. 
- Dependency breadth (multiple buyers/suppliers) reduces single‑source risk. <cite id="02f4d533-3">Diversification across products and buyers in GVCs reduces exclusion from design and dependency, stabilizing margins and growth opportunities</cite>. 
- Structural specialization vs. multi‑purpose design. <cite id="06149198-4">Meatpacking sector disruptions from COVID revealed fragility of specialized, labor‑intensive facilities; resilience implied multi‑purpose layouts, safer designs, and inventory/flow changes</cite> <cite id="06149198-1">Multi‑source, shorter chains fared better than long, specialized chains during extreme events</cite>. 
- Calibrating scale: capacity buffers and lead‑time resilience. <cite id="06149198-2">Simulations indicate 75% capacity increases at centralized fulfillment centers and prioritized delivery lanes can recover profit and reduce lead time under disruptions</cite>.

5. Comparability across studies: when findings agree or conflict
- Converging patterns:
  - Breadth generally boosts resilience up to a point, with inverted‑U relationships common across strategy and operations contexts. <cite id="02f4d533-1">Inverse U‑shaped breadth–resilience under sanctions</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-2">Quadratic survival effects with moderate breadth</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-4">Inverted‑U in patent diversity and profitability</cite>. 
  - Mechanisms are consistent: risk spreading, option value, flexibility, and dependency reduction. <cite id="02f4d533-0">Diversification spreads risk and enables resource shifts and scaling</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-3">Diversified product portfolios reduce input/buyer dependency</cite>. 
  - Capability alignment and coherence are critical; without fit, breadth harms resilience. <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">High‑tech firms benefit from diverse, coherent patent ecosystems; low‑tech firms may prefer specialization</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Related diversification yields strategic resilience when within managerial capacity</cite>.
- Divergences and scope conditions:
  - Industry structure and shocks matter. <cite id="02f4d533-0">In concentrated industries, multi‑market firms grew more during downturns</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-1">Under sanctions, optimal breadth shifted with R&D and ownership</cite>. 
  - Measurement and metric differences change conclusions. <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Resilience outcomes depend on how diversification is measured and whether it matches resources and environment</cite>. <cite id="02f4d533-4">Product development strategies were strongly associated with resilience, whereas market development showed non‑significant effects in SME clusters</cite>. 
  - Supply chain structure and sourcing modality shift trade‑offs. <cite id="06149198-1">Shorter, local, multi‑source chains improved resilience in rural Australia</cite> <cite id="06149198-2">Backup supplier strategies and capacity buffers restored performance in simulations</cite>. 
- Synthesis lens: 
  - If “product‑program size” is too small, firms lack buffers and pivot options; if too large, specialization costs, coordination frictions, and dependency risks erode resilience. Moderate breadth with scalable capabilities and modular architectures tends to be optimal. <cite id="02f4d533-2">Mid breadth maximizes survival rates over time</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">Moderate patent diversity often maximizes innovation/profitability</cite>. 
  - R&D and product development capability act as complements to breadth: they expand option sets and accelerate reconfiguration, but with diminishing returns if concentrated beyond coherence. <cite id="02f4d533-1">R&D increases resilience and amplifies the optimal breadth window</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-4">Resilient firms pivoted via product development leveraging core competencies</cite>.

6. Practical guidance: calibrating product‑program size and range
- Diagnose current breadth and coherence: map product families, customer segments, geographies, and technologies; assess relatedness and capability overlap. <cite id="ff1f28e6-1">Coherent diversification emphasizes relatedness across product–country networks</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Effectiveness depends on matching form to resources and environment</cite>. 
- Target moderate breadth and modularity: balance number of product lines/SKUs against integration costs; design modular platforms to enable fast iteration and fault isolation. <cite id="02f4d533-1">Inverse U‑shaped breadth with R&D complementarity suggests an optimal window</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-2">Patent portfolio diversity should be calibrated to avoid inefficiency at extremes</cite>. 
- Build supply breadth and buffers: diversify suppliers/alternate routes and categories; maintain safety stock where hazards are severe; invest in capacity buffers and prioritized lanes for critical flows. <cite id="06149198-3">Multi‑brand and cooperative sourcing strategies improved resilience</cite> <cite id="06149198-2">Backup suppliers and capacity increases restored performance</cite>. 
- Invest in dynamic capabilities: sustain R&D and product development pipelines aligned to portfolio breadth to support rapid pivots; manage diminishing returns via portfolio governance. <cite id="02f4d533-1">R&D positively affects resilience and sharpens the optimal breadth window</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-4">Resilient firms pivoted quickly via product development leveraging core competencies</cite>. 
- Monitor context shifts: reassess optimal breadth as regulation, trade, and technology regimes change, and as managerial capacity scales. <cite id="02f4d533-1">Ownership and sanction regimes altered optimal breadth</cite> <cite id="ff1f28e6-3">Resilience effects weaken when scope/complexity exceed managerial capacity</cite>.

Bottom line
- Product‑program size and range materially influence resilience: moderate breadth and scale—matched to coherent capabilities and modular supply arrangements—tend to raise survival, continuity, and recovery capacity, while both narrow specialization and excessive breadth degrade resilience via lack of options and rising coordination/dependency risks. <cite id="02f4d533-0">Diversification mechanisms spread risk and enable reallocation and scaling</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-1">Inverse U‑shaped breadth–resilience with R&D amplification</cite> <cite id="02f4d533-2">Quadratic survival effects favor moderate breadth</cite> <cite id="06149198-1">Shorter, multi‑source chains improved resilience in disruptions</cite>.

For SMEs operating in the China-Europe trade corridor, where geopolitical tensions and trade policy uncertainty create periodic disruptions, this resilience benefit carries substantial value.
